# Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 43 (Bi-Vb Pc43)

**ID:** Bi-Vb Pc43
**Section:** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga (bi-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 43
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** 43. Spinning yarn
**Title (English, from literature):** Spinning yarn
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bi-vb-pc43
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul7.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Suttakantana Sikkhāpada* (Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 43) stipulates that a nun who spins yarn commits an offense requiring confession: *yā pana bhikkhunī suttaṁ kanteyya, pācittiyan ti* [SuttaCentral; Hüsken 1997]. As Ute Hüsken notes, there is no corresponding rule in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga [Hüsken 1997]. The permitted materials for yarn in the Vinaya commentary correspond to allowable robe materials, indicating that the spinning was aimed at robe manufacture; functionally, the injunction was formulated to prevent fully ordained nuns from lapsing into secular household labor and female domestic roles [Hüsken 1997].

Under the non-offense (*anāpatti*) provisions, a nun does not incur an offense if she re-spins thread that has already been spun or unravels and corrects poorly spun yarn (*samghāṭetvā kantati dukkantitaṁ vā paṭikantati*) [Hüsken 1997]. In the analysis of offenses (*padabhājanīya*), preliminary preparations such as sorting raw cotton (*kappāsavicinana*) entail an offense of wrong conduct (*dukkaṭa*) for each stage of effort, whereas completing the spinning and winding it onto the spindle incurs the full *pācittiya* [Hüsken 1997].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral demonstrate that this rule was preserved across early Buddhist monastic traditions, with parallels in the Theravāda Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha and Bhikkhunī Parivāra, as well as the Dharmaguptaka (*Lzh Dg Bi Vb Pc 114*), Mahīśāsaka (*Lzh Mi Bi Vb Pc 163*), Sarvāstivāda (*Lzh Sarv Bi Vb Pc 146*), and Mūlasarvāstivāda (*Lzh Mu Bi Vb Pc 155*; Tibetan *xct-mu-bi-vb-pc136*) codes [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus detects 186 internal Pali text-reuse segments across 75 texts, reflecting standard formulaic legal structures shared with other Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga rules, most extensively with Pācittiya 50, Pācittiya 87, and Pācittiya 42 [DharmaNexus]. An English translation is provided by Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral].
